questions.question: A conductor has an ampacity of 95 A. The ampacity does not correspond to a standard overcurrent device rating. What is the maximum standard rating of overcurrent device permitted to protect this conductor under the general rule?
questions.answer: 90 A. Where the conductor ampacity does not correspond to a standard rating, the next LOWER standard size from Table 13 is used; the next standard size below 95 A is 90 A.
solution_steps: Rule 14-104: OCPD rating must not exceed conductor ampacity; if ampacity is between standard sizes use the next LOWER standard size.
Standard sizes (Table 13) around 95 A are 90 A and 100 A; 100 A exceeds the ampacity, so the next lower = 90 A.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a standard ampere rating for a fuse or circuit breaker in Table 13?
questions.answer: 75 A is not a standard rating; the standard sizes jump from 70 A to 80 A to 90 A.
solution_steps: 75 A is absent from the standard list, so it is the correct (non-standard) choice.

questions.question: A solidly grounded service is rated 1200 A at 600Y/347 V. Is equipment ground-fault protection required by Rule 14-102?
options: A) No, voltage is too low
B) No, current is too low
C) Yes, both conditions are met
D) Only if it supplies motors
questions.answer: Yes. The service is 1000 A or more (1200 A) AND exceeds 150 V to ground (347 V), so both conditions of Rule 14-102 are satisfied and GFP is required.
solution_steps: Rule 14-102 requires GFP only when BOTH: rated 1000 A or more AND more than 150 V to ground.
1200 A is at/above 1000 A and 347 V exceeds 150 V to ground; both gates pass, so GFP is required.

questions.question: Where must the overcurrent device protecting a conductor generally be located?
options: A) At the load end of the conductor
B) At the point where the conductor receives its supply
C) Anywhere along the conductor run
D) Only at the main service only
questions.answer: At the point where the conductor receives its supply, so the conductor is protected for its full length (subward tap exceptions aside).
solution_steps: Overcurrent protection is placed at the supply (origin) end so the whole conductor is protected against overcurrent.
Placing it at the load end would leave the conductor unprotected ahead of the device.

questions.question: Under Rule 14-100, overcurrent protection must be provided for which conductors of a circuit?
questions.answer: Each ungrounded (live) conductor must be provided with overcurrent protection.
solution_steps: Rule 14-100 is the foundation rule: every ungrounded conductor must have overcurrent protection.
The grounded/neutral and bonding conductors are not the basis of the requirement.

questions.question: On a 120/240 V single-phase, 3-wire branch circuit supplying a 240 V load such as a water heater, what type of overcurrent device is required for the two ungrounded conductors?
options: A) Two single-pole breakers with no common trip
D) No overcurrent device is required
questions.answer: A 2-pole common-trip breaker, so that both ungrounded conductors of the 240 V load are opened together.
solution_steps: A 240 V load fed by two ungrounded conductors must have both conductors opened simultaneously.
A 2-pole common-trip breaker accomplishes this; two independent single-pole devices could leave one leg energized.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the interrupting rating (interrupting capacity) of an overcurrent device?
options: A) The maximum continuous load it can carry
B) The voltage at which it operates
C) The maximum fault current it can safely interrupt
D) The trip time at rated current
questions.answer: The maximum fault (short-circuit) current the device can safely interrupt without damage.
solution_steps: Rule 14-012: the device must have an interrupting rating at least equal to the available fault current at its point of installation.
Interrupting rating is about safely clearing a short circuit, not continuous load or trip timing.

questions.question: A series-rated (series-combination) arrangement of overcurrent devices is used to:
options: A) Increase the continuous current rating of a panel
B) Eliminate the need for a main breaker
C) Allow a downstream device with a lower individual interrupting rating to be applied where available fault current is higher
questions.answer: Allow a downstream device with a lower individual interrupting rating to be applied where the available fault current exceeds that rating, because the upstream device shares the interrupting duty.
solution_steps: A tested series combination lets an upstream device help the downstream device clear a fault.
This permits a downstream device whose standalone interrupting rating is below the available fault current to be used in that listed combination.

questions.question: For a circuit supplying a cyclic or motor load that produces inrush, what general class of fuse is selected under Rule 14-212 to avoid nuisance opening?
questions.answer: A time-delay (dual-element / HRC time-delay) fuse, which rides through inrush without opening.
solution_steps: Rule 14-212: fuses for cyclic/inrush loads must be time-delay type so normal inrush does not open them.
Fast-acting fuses would nuisance-trip on motor or heating inrush.

questions.question: An overcurrent device must be marked so that which of the following is identifiable?
options: A) Its ampere rating and interrupting rating
C) The length of the conductor it protects
questions.answer: Its ampere rating and interrupting rating must be marked/identifiable on the device.
solution_steps: Devices carry markings for ampere rating and interrupting capacity so the correct device can be verified for the application.
Installer name, conductor length, and room temperature are not device markings.

questions.question: A No. 8 AWG copper RW90 (used at 75 degC column) conductor has an ampacity of 50 A from Table 2. For a non-continuous load, what is the maximum standard overcurrent device rating that may protect it?
questions.answer: 50 A. The conductor ampacity (50 A) is itself a standard size, so the maximum overcurrent device is 50 A.
solution_steps: Table 2: No. 8 Cu at 75 degC = 50 A.
Rule 14-104: set OCPD at conductor ampacity; 50 A is a standard Table 13 size, so the maximum device = 50 A.

questions.question: A solidly grounded service is rated 1000 A at 208Y/120 V. Is equipment ground-fault protection required by Rule 14-102?
options: A) Yes, the current condition is met
B) Yes, both conditions are met
D) No, it does not exceed 150 V to ground
questions.answer: No. Although the service is 1000 A, 208Y/120 V is only 120 V to ground, which does not exceed 150 V, so GFP is not required.
solution_steps: Rule 14-102 needs BOTH 1000 A or more AND more than 150 V to ground.
120 V to ground is at/below 150 V, so the voltage gate fails and GFP is not required.

questions.question: A circuit breaker used as a switch to regularly turn a load on and off (switch duty) must be marked:
options: B) SWD or HID as applicable
questions.answer: SWD (switching duty) or HID where applicable, indicating it is suitable for regular switching of the load.
solution_steps: Breakers used for routine on/off switching of lighting loads must be marked for switch duty (SWD), or HID for high-intensity discharge lighting.
HACR and GFCI markings denote different functions.

questions.question: Unless marked otherwise, what symmetrical interrupting rating is assumed for a moulded-case circuit breaker?
questions.answer: 10 000 A symmetrical is the default interrupting rating unless the breaker is specifically marked with a higher value.
solution_steps: Rule 14-606: a breaker's interrupting rating is taken as 10 000 A symmetrical unless marked otherwise.
Higher ratings (22 kA, 42 kA, etc.) apply only when so marked.

questions.question: Equipment ground-fault protection installed under Rule 14-102 must operate to clear a ground-fault current of 3000 A or more within a maximum of:
questions.answer: 1 second. A ground-fault current of 3000 A or more must be cleared within a maximum of 1 second.
solution_steps: Rule 14-102 sets the maximum clearing time for equipment GFP.
For a ground-fault current of 3000 A or more, that maximum time is 1 second.
